inline.s: Zi 3: Raising the fruit-virtue to bring faith in the mind of cause.
The ocean of right universal knowledge of the Buddhas is born from the mind and thought.

By 'right universal knowledge' is meant one of the ten epithets of a Buddha. The transcendent Dharma is fully and exhaustively known by it. Deep and vast without limit, therefore it is likened to an ocean. The Buddha's virtues are boundless; the text gives but a brief mention of universal knowledge in order to embrace the rest. The ten thousand virtues of the fruit-person all arise from mind and thought; the intent is to encourage lower ordinary beings to single-mindedly and diligently cultivate, so that their effort is not in vain. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Zi 4: Concluding exhortation to cultivate the cause, which must rely on the fruit-virtue.
Therefore one should single-mindedly hold the thought and contemplate intently that Buddha: Tathagata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha.

It is precisely because the virtue of the Buddha contemplated is lofty and deep that he urges the holding of the thought. The preceding passage spoke generally of all Buddhas; this one points specifically to Amitabha, concluding and returning to the true intent of this sutra. Hence it says 'contemplate intently that Buddha.' Tathagata is translated as 'Thus-come'; Arhat, 'worthy of offerings'; Samyaksambuddha, 'right universal knowledge.' These are three of the ten epithets, briefly mentioned. The detailed explanation is given elsewhere. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Gui 2: Properly clarifying the method of contemplating the Buddha, in two parts.
First, directly contemplating the three images.
Second, the realm of the accomplished contemplation.
Zi 1: Directly contemplating the three images, in two parts.
First, contemplating the image of the Buddha.
Second, contemplating the images of the two bodhisattvas.
Chou 1: Contemplating the image of the Buddha, in two parts.
First, properly clarifying the contemplation of the image.
Second, seeing the land through the image.
Yin 1: Properly clarifying the contemplation of the image.
In thinking of that Buddha, one should first visualize the image; whether the eyes are closed or open, one sees a jewel image, Jambunada golden in color, seated upon that lotus.

The image is used to represent the real, going from the easy to the difficult; therefore, whether painted or carved, according to what a person is familiar seeing, that is taken as the object. 'Seated on that lotus' refers to the lotus seat of the preceding contemplation. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Yin 2: Seeing the land through the image.

Having seen the image seated, the mind's eye opens. Clearly and distinctly one sees the Land of Ultimate Bliss adorned with seven jewels: jewel ground, jewel pools, jewel trees in rows, jewel canopies of the devas spread above, and nets of many jewels filling the sky. Seeing these things, one makes them utterly clear, as if viewing something in the palm of the hand.

Seeing the land through the image is seeing the retributive environment of the preceding contemplation. Miaozong's commentary says: 'Once the image-contemplation is accomplished, the mind's eye opens, and one sees broadly the features of the retributive environment, the ground, the trees, and so forth. One should know that these trees and so on exceed those of the preceding contemplation by countless times. Why is this? Because the present jewel image must match the lotus seat; if the trees were not tall, how could they cover the seat? All this is because the wondrous contemplation becomes ever deeper, so that what is contemplated becomes ever more excellent.' Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Viewing in the palm of the hand' speaks of its clarity.
Chou 2: Contemplating the images of the two bodhisattvas.

Having seen this, one should further create a great lotus on the Buddha's left, like the preceding lotus, identical in every way. Again create a great lotus on the Buddha's right. Visualize the image of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva seated on the left lotus seat, also golden in color, just as before, without difference. Visualize the image of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva seated on the right lotus seat.

First, contemplating the lotus seat. 'Like the preceding lotus' refers to the one the Buddha sits on. Considering the bodies of the bodhisattvas, the lotus should be reckoned as smaller. Next, contemplating the form and image. 'Also golden in color' means the bodhisattvas' bodies are the same color as the preceding Buddha. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Zi 2: The realm of the accomplished contemplation, in two parts.
First, the eye beholds the supreme realm.
Second, the ear hears the wondrous Dharma.
Chou 1: The eye beholds the supreme realm.

When this contemplation is accomplished, the images of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas all emit light. That light is golden, illuminating the many jewel trees. Beneath each tree there are also three lotuses, and upon each lotus there is one image of a Buddha and two images of bodhisattvas, filling that land completely.
First, the three images emit light, and the light-color illuminates the trees. Next, beneath each tree one sees the three images everywhere, present in every place. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Chou 2: The ear hears the wondrous Dharma.

When this contemplation is accomplished, the practitioner should hear the flowing water and light, as well as the many jewel trees, ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks, all speaking the wondrous Dharma. Whether emerging from or entering absorption, he constantly hears the wondrous Dharma. What the practitioner has heard, upon emerging from absorption, he recollects and holds without letting go, making it accord with the sutras. If it does not accord, it is called deluded thinking. If it does accord, it is called a coarse thought seeing the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

First, this clarifies hearing the Dharma within the contemplation. The flowing water and light, together with the many jewel trees, are the insentient speaking the Dharma; the ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks are the sentient speaking the Dharma. That the sentient and the insentient alike perfectly fulfill the Buddha-wisdom of the seed-nature may be seen here. (Lingzhi's commentary: 'Bitter, empty, impermanent, and no-self, the perfections, hence it is called the wondrous Dharma.') The practitioner does not merely hear it upon entering absorption; so too upon emerging from it; hence it says he constantly hears. Second, from 'the practitioner' onward, it clarifies that what is heard should accord with the sutras, otherwise it is delusion. Hence it says, 'If it does not accord, it is called deluded thinking; if it accords, it is called a coarse seeing.' This clarifies the state upon emerging from absorption. Because when hearing within absorption it necessarily accords with the sutras (Lingzhi's commentary: 'This means the dharma heard does not conflict with the scriptural teachings, hence it is called according.'). Fearing that upon emerging it might not be so, this instruction is given. If upon emerging it still accords with the sutras, then it is not emerging yet, emerging, and emerging yet, not emerging. Even so, it is still called a coarse thought, because comparing the image to the real, one must distinguish coarse from subtle. This contemplation is an expedient of the Buddha-contemplation; how could it be wholly identical with the true Buddha-contemplation? (The Yanyi) Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Contradicting the teachings is delusion; according with the Dharma is still coarse. Compared with the following samadhi, coarse and subtle are distinguished here.'
Question: The sutra says 'the heard dharma he recollects and holds without letting go.' What if one has not heard it?

Answer: One must attain superior absorption before one can hear it. If one does not hear it, then one may take up the fifth contemplation, the so-called water-sound expounding the bitter, empty, impermanent, and no-self perfections, and the birds' praise of the Three Jewels; relying on these, one recollects and holds, without contravening the scriptural teachings. (The Shilun)

The sutra says: 'In thinking of that Buddha, one should first visualize the image.' The word 'first' indicates that visualizing the image and thinking of the Buddha are two tasks. From 'next, think of the Buddha' down to 'arising from the mind of thought,' all these suggest thinking of the Buddha's awesome virtue. What are awesome virtue and virtue? 'The ocean of right universal knowledge' is the awesome; great compassion is the virtue. Having thought of the Buddha's wisdom, vast as an ocean, one then contemplates the Buddha's mind of compassion without conditions. The image must be contemplated first: mentally create a jewel image of Jambunada golden color, with the two bodhisattvas each seated upon a lotus; all the images emit light, illuminating the many jewel trees. The reflected images beneath each tree are all alike. The eighth contemplation is confined to this; one need not seek the thirty-two marks and eighty minor marks in their various parts. Contemplating the Buddha has a direct function for perfuming the seed-nature. The Record on Consciousness-Only says: 'The self-nature's immediate cause is called the equally-flowing seed; the different-nature attraction is called the ripening seed; all seeds are fully contained within these two.' The equally-flowing includes both the defiled and the undefiled; the ripening is only the defiled. Contemplating the Buddha is a transcendent Dharma, not contained in the ripening, and should belong to the equally-flowing. The Mahayana-samgraha says: 'The teachings and such that flow from the most pure Dharma-realm are called the equally-flowing of the most pure Dharma-realm.' According to this, one who contemplates the Buddha has, in the near term, the cause of rebirth in the Pure Land, and in the far term, the cause of Buddhahood after asamkhya kalpas. This is what is meant by being drawn by one's own kind, for the fruit resembles the cause. Yet the practitioner must purify his mind at all times; if the time of being tainted by habits is much while the time of contemplating the Buddha is little, the quantities being so unequal, it will lack the supreme function. The Vimalakirti Sutra says: 'As the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure' - this is truly an unchanging principle. (The Shilun)
Gui 3: Concluding statement.
This is the visualization of the image, called the eighth contemplation.
Gui 4: Manifesting the benefit.
Those who make this contemplation remove the offenses of birth and death of immeasurable millions of kalpas; in this very body they attain the Buddha-mindfulness samadhi.

The passage has two points: first, removing the obstacle of offenses; second, approaching the samadhi, which is the following Buddha-contemplation. If the image-contemplation is accomplished, the true body will surely be seen; hence it says in this very body one attains it. (Lingzhi's commentary)

blocks.text: Xin 3: Directly Contemplating the Buddha's Body (the Ninth, the Buddha-Body Contemplation), in Five Parts

inline.s: First, concluding the preceding and arousing the following.
Second, properly showing the body's marks; Third, raising the benefit and urging cultivation; Fourth, concluding the contemplation's name; Fifth, distinguishing right and wrong contemplation.
Ren 1: Concluding the preceding and arousing the following.
The Buddha told Ananda and Queen Vaidehi: 'Once this contemplation is accomplished, next you should contemplate the marks and light of the body of the Buddha of Measureless Life.'

This sentence concludes the preceding; the next sentence arouses the following. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'This, like the image-contemplation, has the sequential text of treading on the preceding and arousing the following; the intent is that proper cultivation may not take a different path.'
Ren 2: Properly showing the marks of the body, in three parts.
First, separately distinguishing the body's marks.
Second, generally showing the marks and virtues; Third, the realm of the accomplished contemplation.
Gui 1: Separately distinguishing the body's marks.

Ananda, you should know: the body of the Buddha of Measureless Life is like the Jambunada gold of the Yama heavens, in its hundreds of millions and billions; the Buddha's body is sixty trillion nayuta Ganges-sands yojanas in height. The white hair between the brows is coiled clockwise, like five Mount Sumerus. The Buddha's eyes are like the water of the four great oceans, clear blue and distinct. From all the pores of the body issues light, like Mount Sumeru. That Buddha's halo is like a hundred billion thousand-times-great-thousand worlds. Within the halo are a million billion nayuta Ganges-sands transformation-buddhas; each transformation-buddha also has many, countless transformation-bodhisattvas as attendants.

First, contemplating the color of the Buddha's body. Zhizhi's commentary says: 'The gold of the Yama heavens surpasses the sun and moon by doubling their radiance into thousands of millions, a splendor beyond thought!' Next, from 'the Buddha's body,' one contemplates the body's measure. Zhizhi's commentary says: 'Nayuta is a number reaching the myriad; here it means tens of thousands of millions. Yojana is a measure; the greater is eighty li, the middle sixty li, the lesser forty li. Compared with the two great bodhisattvas, the Buddha is less by twenty trillion nayutas, but more by Ganges-sands times.' Lingzhi's commentary says: 'The Buddha's body is measureless, while the capacities' perceptions differ; those cited in the text are but borrowed quantities, to show it is without quantity, and to make clear the Buddha's body cannot be fixed. Hence the passage below says: As previously said, the measure of the Buddha of Measureless Life is without bound, beyond the reach of the mind and power of ordinary beings. Again it says: Or he manifests a great body filling the sky. Citing this verifies the preceding, so one knows it is without limit. To measure the ocean with a ladle, to measure the sky with a foot-rule, is that possible? The simile makes this clear.'

Third, from 'between the brows' onward, the measure of the brow-hair. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Coiled clockwise, its shape like a pearl. One Sumeru is three million three hundred sixty thousand li high; its breadth and length likewise. Five Sumerus make sixteen million eight hundred thousand li.' Fourth, from 'the Buddha's eyes,' the measure of the eyes' color. Lingzhi's commentary: 'One great ocean is eighty-four thousand yojanas; the four great oceans together make three hundred thirty-six thousand yojanas.' Fifth, from 'all the body,' the flowing light from the pores. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'To stream is to flow; the light from each pore is like Mount Sumeru.' Zhizhi's commentary: 'The light like Mount Sumeru is because it possesses the color of many jewels.' Sixth, from 'That Buddha,' the halo's transformation-buddhas. Zhizhi's commentary: 'First, the measure. The thousand-times-great-thousand worlds, again with a hundred billion; the all-round measure can be known. Within the halo, next, the transformation-buddhas; within each, third, the transformed assemblies.'
Gui 2: Generally showing the marks and virtues.

The Buddha of Measureless Life has eighty-four thousand marks; within each mark there are eighty-four thousand subsidiary marks; within each subsidiary mark there are again eighty-four thousand lights. Each light universally illumines the beings of the ten directions who are mindful of the Buddha, gathering them without abandoning. These lights, marks, and transformation-buddhas cannot be fully told. One should only recollect and visualize them, so that the mind's eye sees them.

First, properly clarifying the marks and virtues. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'A body of sixteen feet possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor marks; now the measure of the body, marks, virtues, and lights of Amitabha, all of eighty-four thousand, their number is without limit, beyond counting!' Zhizhi's commentary says: 'All being eighty-four thousand is because he turns the dust-like defilement into the virtue of wisdom.' Miaozong's commentary says: 'The marks, virtues, and lights are all said to be eighty-four thousand, because manifesting virtue from the obstacle produces this number. The Buddha, dwelling at the stage of the ordinary being, is endowed with eighty-four thousand defilements; within all these defilements he sees the real marks. Since principle and wisdom accord, he can manifest the marks, virtues, and lights; hence each clause gives such a number. The practitioner contemplating now, knowing in his mind that this is so, can see the Buddha's marks within the defilements.'

Next, from 'each light,' it clarifies the gathering of beings. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Below it shows the light universally illumining and gathering beings; this is the very mind-substance of Amitabha's compassion.' Zhizhi's commentary says: 'The Buddha thinks of beings as a mother remembers her child; hence within the marks, each light illumines and gathers the one mindful of the Buddha.' Miaozong's commentary says: 'Beings and the Buddha are of one substance; although the land is vast and beings many, the gathering misses none.' The Yuelun says: 'That light universally illumines the beings of the ten directions who are mindful of the Buddha and gathers them without abandoning; hence one knows that when beings mindfully invoke the Buddha in a single thought, they are constantly within the great compassionate light of our Buddha, whether sitting, lying, or walking, without the least separation.'
Question: For those who do not invoke the Buddha, does the Buddha's light gather them?

Answer: Whether one invokes or does not invoke, there is nothing the light does not gather. But the invoker of the Buddha, being in accord with the light, is gathered for rebirth and surely never falls back. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: 'It is like fish roe; if the mother does not attend to them, the roe rots.' The Surangama Sutra says, 'The Buddha thinks of beings as a mother remembers her child.' It is only that the child, toward the mother, either remembers or does not. Again it is like a blind man beneath the sun: the sun illumines all, but the blind man does not see. Those who do not invoke the Buddha are likewise. (Lingzhi's commentary)

Third, from 'that light,' it generally distinguishes the inscrutable. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Its light and marks, together with the two lights of the upper body and the nape (the nape being the halo); the transformation-buddhas are what the halo manifests. Words cannot exhaust it; only by recollecting and visualizing is it seen. The mind's eye is the mind-thought.'
Gui 3: The realm of the accomplished contemplation.
Those who see this see all the Buddhas of the ten directions. Because they see the Buddhas, it is called the Buddha-mindfulness samadhi.

This clarifies that contemplating one Buddha, one sees all Buddhas. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Seeing many Buddhas, because the Dharma-body is the same. The Buddha-mindfulness samadhi gets its name from this.'

Those who make this contemplation are said to contemplate the bodies of all Buddhas. Because they contemplate the Buddha's body, they also see the Buddha's mind. The Buddha's mind is great compassion. With the unconditional compassion they gather all beings.

This clarifies that contemplating the Buddha's body, one sees the Buddha's mind. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Seeing the Buddha's mind, because the body is the mark of the mind. The Buddha has no mind of selfish inclinations; he has only great compassion. Compassion is giving joy; mercy is removing suffering. As beings are inexhaustible, the Buddha's great compassion is likewise inexhaustible. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: Compassion has three kinds. First, the being-referencing compassion: with no deliberate clinging to all beings, yet it naturally benefits them. Second, the Dharma-referencing compassion: with no deliberate contemplation of Dharma, yet it naturally counteracts with regard to all dharmas. Third, the unconditional compassion: with no deliberate contemplation of principle, yet it naturally abides in the equal highest truth. The last raises the principle-substance; the first two concern the functional use. Now raising the unconditional, the meaning includes all three. That is, the minds of all Buddhas abide neither in being nor in non-being, neither relying on the three times; the equal great compassion constantly illumines the Dharma-realm. With this it gathers beings, and no being is not gathered. It does not arise through conditions, hence it is called unconditional. This is what was earlier said: gathering the beings mindful of the Buddha without abandoning.' Zhizhi's commentary says: 'From contemplating, next, one contemplates the Buddha's mind. First raising the contemplation of the body, it is entirely the compassionate mind responding and manifesting; hence it says contemplating the body, seeing the mind. Affection and joyful remembrance is compassion, the virtue of giving joy; pity and distress is mercy, the virtue of removing suffering. Each has three aspects: first, the being-referencing compassion, taking hold of all beings as parents and six relatives; second, the Dharma-referencing compassion, taking hold of all dharmas as all arising from causes and conditions; third, the unconditional compassion, abiding neither in the marks of Dharma nor in the marks of beings. The three of mercy are to be understood likewise. The Buddha's mind is formless, manifesting through the virtue of inherent nature; hence it is said to be great compassion. He employs the compassion of the same body to save all beings, yet neither takes hold of the marks of beings nor limits the number of kalpas; hence it is called unconditional compassion gathering beings. The Samadhi Sutra says: The minds of all Buddhas are great compassion. That which compassion takes as its object is beings in suffering. When it sees beings experiencing suffering, it is like an arrow entering the heart, wishing to pull out their suffering. Since all Buddhas take beings as their body and mind, then outward is the Tathagata's body and inward is the mind, and beings may all follow and contemplate them accordingly.'
Ren 3: Raising the benefit and urging cultivation, in four parts.
First, properly clarifying the benefit.
Second, urging the cultivation of the contemplation; Third, showing the contemplation method; Fourth, again raising the benefit.
Gui 1: Properly clarifying the benefit.
Those who make this contemplation, when they leave this body in another life, are born before the Buddhas and attain the patience with the unborn.

Leaving this body in another life, having been born in that land, one directly realizes the unborn; hence one knows that if this contemplation is accomplished, the highest-grade highest rebirth is clear. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Gui 2: Urging the cultivation of the contemplation.
Therefore the wise one should bind the mind and contemplate intently the Buddha of Measureless Life.

The wise one is the person who cultivates the contemplation. Relying on the preceding contemplation methods, this is the intent contemplation. Because by cultivating this contemplation one is reborn and attains the patience, the merit is deep and the benefit great, hence he urges binding the mind. Thus in the Pratyutpanna Sutra, beings ask the Buddha: 'For what cause are we born in this land?' Amitabha answers: 'By cultivating the Buddha-mindfulness samadhi, one is born in that land.' (Lingzhi's commentary)
Gui 3: Showing the contemplation method.

Those who contemplate the Buddha of Measureless Life enter through a single mark. They need only contemplate the white hair between the brows, making it utterly clear. Those who see the mark of the white hair between the brows will find the eighty-four thousand marks and virtues naturally appear.

'Many marks self-endowed' - because the single mark of the brow-hair sums up all the marks. According to the sutra text, one contemplates the measure of five Sumerus. Hence it says 'the eighty-four thousand marks and virtues naturally appear.' One then knows it is not the brow-hair of the sixteen-foot body. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Gui 4: Again raising the benefit.
Those who see the Buddha of Measureless Life see the measureless Buddhas of the ten directions. Because one sees the measureless Buddhas, the Buddhas appear before one and give the prophecy.
Lingzhi's commentary says: 'The many Buddhas giving the prophecy - one receives their seal of approval and the prophecy of becoming a Buddha.'
Ren 4: Concluding the contemplation's name.
This is the universal contemplation of the marks of all the form-bodies, called the ninth contemplation.
Lingzhi's commentary says: 'The word all either refers collectively to the Buddhas seen, or specifically to the marks of Amitabha; both explanations are acceptable.'

blocks.text: Geng 2: Contemplating the Buddha's Attendants, in Two Parts

inline.s: First, contemplating Avalokitesvara.
Second, contemplating Mahasthamaprapta.
Xin 1: Contemplating Avalokitesvara (the Tenth, the Avalokitesvara Contemplation), in Five Parts.
First, concluding the preceding and arousing the following.
Second, properly showing the body's marks; Third, concluding the contemplation's name; Fourth, raising the benefit and urging cultivation; Fifth, distinguishing right and wrong contemplation.
The Buddha told Ananda and Queen Vaidehi: 'Having seen the Buddha of Measureless Life clearly and distinctly, next you should also contemplate Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva.'
Ren 2: Properly showing the body's marks.
This bodhisattva's body is eighty trillion nayuta yojanas tall. The body is purple-gold in color. On the top of the head is the fleshy top-knot.

First, clarifying the body's measure. Zhizhi's commentary says: 'Its measure is less than the Buddha's body by Ganges-sands; for example, in the realm of Pure Light Adornment of the east, the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King of Wisdom has a body of six million eight hundred thousand yojanas; Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound has forty-two thousand yojanas (see the Wondrous Sound chapter of the Lotus Sutra). In this land, our Tathagata Shakyamuni is sixteen feet, while a person is eight feet.' The Shilun says: 'This contemplation first speaks of the body's measure as eighty trillion nayuta yojanas. Now the Buddha's body is sixty trillion nayuta Ganges-sands yojanas. Speaking in trillions, eighty is more than sixty; speaking in yojanas, without the words Ganges-sands, it is reduced greatly. Yet in such places one need not cling; one should only imagine the body's height as resembling the Buddha's, only slightly lower.' 'The body purple-gold' - second, clarifying the body's color. 'On the top of the head' - third, clarifying the top-knot. The annotated commentary says: 'The fleshy top-knot, in Sanskrit ushnisha, is a mound of flesh on the top of the Buddha's head, shaped like a top-knot, hence called the fleshy top-knot. It is one of the thirty-two marks.'

At the nape there is a halo, its face on each side a hundred thousand yojanas. Within that halo are five hundred transformation-buddhas, like Shakyamuni. Each transformation-buddha has five hundred transformation-bodhisattvas and measureless devas as attendants.

Fourth, clarifying the nape-light. The Yanyi says: 'The light's measure on the four faces is each a hundred hundred-thousand (that is, one hundred thousand) yojanas. Within it are transformation-buddhas; each Buddha has transformation-bodhisattvas, and further there are devas as attendants, their number measureless.' Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Like Shakyamuni refers to the sixteen-foot body.'
Within the light of the whole body, all the forms of beings of the five paths appear.

Fifth, the body-light. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'The beings of the five paths, because the asuras are combined in. The bodhisattva manifests his form in the five paths to save suffering beings; hence within the light their forms appear.' The Shilun says: 'Within the light are not only transformation-buddhas and bodhisattvas, but also the five paths, extending to the evil destinies; because this bodhisattva's original vow, clad in the armor of the great vow, travels through all the realms to save suffering beings. He is not like the Buddha of Measureless Life, who establishes a Pure Land and takes gathering beings as his principal task.'
On the top of the head, the Virinca mani-jewel forms the heavenly crown. Within that heavenly crown is a standing transformation-buddha, twenty-five yojanas tall.

Sixth, the heavenly crown. The Yanyi says: 'Sakyavirinca is translated as able to prevail. Within the crown is a standing Buddha, twenty-five yojanas tall.' Lingzhi's commentary says: 'The transformation-buddha within the crown represents bearing the fruit while practicing the cause.'

The face of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva is like Jambunada gold. The mark of the hair between the brows possesses the color of the seven jewels, and flows out into eighty-four thousand kinds of light; each light has measureless, countless hundreds of thousands of transformation-buddhas; each transformation-buddha has countless transformation-bodhisattvas as attendants. The transformations are free, filling the worlds of the ten directions.

Seventh, contemplating the face's color. Eighth, from 'between the brows,' the brow-mark. The hair possesses the color of the seven jewels; the color has eighty thousand lights; each light has countless transformation-buddhas; each Buddha has countless transformation-bodhisattvas as attendants. The transformations are free, filling the sky. (The Yanyi)
The Shilun says: 'The brow-mark between the brows makes the color of the seven jewels, different from the white hair.'
The arms are the color of the red lotus. There are eighty hundred-million subtle lights forming a necklace. Within that necklace all the magnificent adornments appear universally.
Ninth, the arm-mark. Its color is like the red lotus. Further there are eighty hundred-million subtle lights forming a necklace; within the necklace all the adornments appear. (The Yanyi)

The palms make the color of five hundred hundred-million mixed lotuses. On the ten finger-tips, each finger-tip has eighty-four thousand lines, like seal-inscriptions. Each line has eighty-four thousand colors; each color has eighty-four thousand lights. That light is gentle, universally illumining all. With these jewel-hands he gathers and leads beings.

Tenth, the hand-mark. The palm is like the color of mixed lotuses. The ten finger-tips each have eighty-four thousand lines; the lines have eighty-four thousand colors; the colors have eighty-four thousand lights; the light illumines all and gathers and leads beings. (The Yanyi)

The Shilun says: 'Throughout the body the parts are not all the same in color. The face is Jambunada gold, the body purple-gold, the arms lotus-red, the hands the color of five hundred hundred-million mixed lotuses; and the jewel-hands have especially many distinguishing colors, representing the virtue of direct gathering and leading. This should be noted.'

When he lifts his foot, beneath the foot is the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel, naturally transforming into five hundred hundred-million light-platforms. When the foot is set down, vajra-mani flowers scatter everywhere, filling without exception.

Eleventh, the foot-mark. If the foot were not lifted, it seems one could not contemplate it; hence one must, when the foot is lifted, contemplate the thousand-spoked wheel. (Lingzhi's commentary: 'The wheel has a thousand spokes, hence named the thousand-spoked wheel.') The wheel-mark transforms into light-platforms. When the foot is set down there are vajra-jewel flowers, spread everywhere. The marks and virtues of the whole body are in general like this. (The Yanyi)

The other marks of the body are fully endowed with the many good marks, no different from the Buddha. Only the fleshy top-knot on the head and the mark of the unseen crown are less than the World-Honored One's.

This clarifies that the other marks are the same as the Buddha's; only the fleshy top-knot differs. Miaozong's commentary says: 'The fleshy top-knot is a mark; the unseen crown is a good mark. These marks and virtues represent the ultimate fruit; now as one in the causal stage, therefore he is not equal to the Buddha.'
Ren 3: Concluding the contemplation's name.
This is the contemplation of the real form-body of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, called the tenth contemplation.
Lingzhi's commentary: 'The real form-body is the response-body.'
Ren 4: Raising the benefit and urging cultivation.

The Buddha told Ananda: 'If one wishes to contemplate Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, one should make this contemplation. Those who make this contemplation do not meet any calamities and are cleansed of the obstacles of karma; they remove the offenses of birth and death of countless kalpas. For such a bodhisattva, merely hearing his name obtains measureless merit - how much more the intent contemplation.'

First, the exhortation on dispelling offenses through cultivating the contemplation. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Should make this means the above various marks; one may not differ. Not meeting calamities removes present difficulties; removing the offenses of countless kalpas breaks past karma.' Next, the exhortation on gaining merit through invoking the name. The Yanyi says: 'Even invoking the name, a scattered-good, still obtains measureless merit - how much more cultivating the contemplation, a concentrated-good, which can remove the grave offenses of birth and death of countless kalpas.' Gaining merit by hearing the name is widely explained in the Universal Gateway chapter.

If one wishes to contemplate Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, first contemplate the fleshy top-knot on the head, next the heavenly crown; the other marks one contemplates in order as well. Make them all clear, as if viewing in the palm of the hand.

Third, showing the order of the contemplation. Lingzhi's commentary: 'From top to bottom is taken as the order.' The Yanyi: 'This means from the crown and nape one follows the order down, right to the wheel-mark beneath the feet, making all clear and distinct, as in the palm of one's hand one sees the lines of one's own palm.' The commentary says: 'Since the body-marks are many, which mark should one first contemplate? Now it shows: first contemplate the fleshy top-knot, next the heavenly crown. Because these two can, in particular, represent Avalokitesvara's virtue-marks. Why? The fleshy top-knot, lower than the Buddha, manifests the practice of the cause; the crown has a transformation-Buddha, manifesting the fruit accomplished of old. If the particular marks are manifest, the remaining general marks then become easy to understand. The practitioner, contemplating the crown, top-knot, brow-hair, face, body-color, and light, must each time use the mind's making and mind's being as the contemplative faculty. The teaching was given before the images, and is applied here. Since it says making the Buddha, one is the Buddha - how could one not be able to make Avalokitesvara, and be Avalokitesvara? Making the top-knot and the crown, being the top-knot and the crown, may all serve as examples. Not only should one use the Buddha as an example to contemplate the bodhisattvas, but one should also apply it to the universal, the miscellaneous, and the three grades; not only use the preceding as example for the following, but also use the following as example for the preceding. This is so that the practitioner may cultivate the contemplation on both the beginning and the end of the sutra text.'
Those who make this contemplation are called right contemplation. If one makes other contemplations, they are called wrong contemplation.

blocks.text: Xin 2: Contemplating Mahasthamaprapta (the Eleventh, the Mahasthamaprapta Contemplation), in Four Parts

inline.s: First, properly clarifying the contemplated realm.
Second, concluding the contemplation's name; Third, manifesting the contemplation's benefit; Fourth, jointly concluding the two contemplations.
First, contemplating the body-marks.
Second, contemplating the action-marks; Third, contemplating the sitting-mark.
Gui 1: Contemplating the body-marks.

Next, contemplate Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva: this bodhisattva's body, in size and measure, is also like Avalokitesvara's. The halo, on each face, is a hundred twenty-five yojanas, illumining two hundred fifty yojanas. The light of the whole body illumines the lands of the ten directions, in purple-gold color. Beings with conditions all see it. Merely seeing the light of a single pore of this bodhisattva, one sees the pure and wondrous light of the measureless Buddhas of the ten directions. Therefore this bodhisattva is named Measureless Light. With the light of wisdom he universally illumines all, causing them to leave the three evil paths and obtain the supreme power; therefore this bodhisattva is named Mahasthamaprapta, Great Power Attained.

The first sentence is the general heading. Below that is the particular explanation. First, clarifying the body-measure. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Like Avalokitesvara - also eighty trillion nayuta.'

Second, the halo. Third, the body-light, which has three: first, the light-color; second, the light's function, meaning beings with conditions see it. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Those who cultivate this contemplation are the beings with conditions.' Third, the two reasons for the name: first, named from the light; second, named from the awesome power. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Because the light illumines beings, removing suffering and giving joy, the name is taken from the awesome power. The supreme power is the ten powers.'

The Shilun says: 'This bodhisattva's body-marks are for the most part wholly without difference from Avalokitesvara's. Now I briefly explain the particular marks; the shared marks I will not repeat. Now the halo of Avalokitesvara is a hundred thousand yojanas - hundred thousand, in Chinese speech is an indefinite great number, but spoken in Western terms it is one hundred thousand. Why then is Mahasthamaprapta's light only a hundred twenty-five yojanas? This is not that the lights have superior and inferior, but that their forms and functions differ. The pores are indeed minute and fine, yet seeing the light of a single pore of this bodhisattva, one sees the pure and wondrous light of the measureless Buddhas of the ten directions - it does not depend on the size of the halo-mark. Moreover, it can cause beings with conditions to all see it; then its function is wondrous indeed.'

This bodhisattva's heavenly crown has five hundred jewel-flowers. Each jewel-flower has five hundred jewel-platforms. Within each platform, the broad and long forms of the pure and wondrous Buddha-lands of the ten directions all appear.
Fourth, the heavenly crown. Zhizhi's commentary says: 'The flowers are lotuses.' The rest is as the text makes known.
The fleshy top-knot on the head is like the padma flower. Upon the fleshy top-knot there is a jewel vase holding various lights, universally manifesting the Buddha's work.
Fifth, the fleshy top-knot. First, clarifying the top-knot's color. Padma is translated as the red lotus. Next, the vase-light's transformations.
The remaining marks of the body are without difference, like Avalokitesvara's.
Sixth, pointing out that the remaining marks are the same as Avalokitesvara's; that is, the face, arms, hands, and so forth.
Gui 2: Contemplating the action-marks.

When this bodhisattva walks, all the worlds of the ten directions tremble. Wherever the earth quakes, there are five hundred hundred-million jewel-flowers. Each jewel-flower is adorned, lofty and manifest, like the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

This means when the bodhisattva walks, the earth of the ten directions quakes; wherever it quakes, jewel-flowers appear. The flowers' loftiness is like the Land of Ultimate Bliss and such. (The Yanyi)
